w: 1 Best candidates: deep, narrow, 3-wall defects Review guide · 7 questions in the bank Infrabony defects are classified by the number of bony walls, their width and their depth (Reynolds, AAP Regeneration Workshop, 2015). The classification drawing numbers the walls in each zone: one defect often combines them, with three walls deep in the defect and fewer toward the crest, and a 1-wall defect between two teeth is a hemiseptum. Defects with a depth greater than 3 mm and a radiographic defect angle of 25 degrees or less were reported to be most amenable to conventional GTR-based regeneration. A 2021 systematic review (Nibali) agrees: deeper defects with narrower angles and more walls showed more CAL gain and radiographic bone gain 12 months after regenerative surgery. In its pooled numbers, defects shallower than 4 mm gained about 0.75 mm less bone, defects with an angle under 37 degrees about 0.94 mm more, and a 1-wall defect about 1.2 mm less bone than a 3-wall one (about 0.6 mm less than a 2-wall). Depth had the strongest evidence. The walls and a narrow angle contain the defect: they hold the clot and graft in place, bring cells and blood vessels in from more surfaces, and hold up the flap. The exam-review guide puts it simply: 3-wall defects are the best candidates. 2 Biologics: EMD (amelogenins), rhPDGF-BB, β-TCP Review guide · 5 questions in the bank Biologics. Enamel matrix derivative (EMD) is an extract of enamel matrix proteins, mostly amelogenins, the proteins involved in enamel formation and periodontal attachment formation during tooth development. Used alone or with a graft, it gives outcomes similar to GTR; the deck shows a case healing with EMD from 2022 to 2025. rhPDGF-BB, recombinant human platelet-derived growth factor BB, is chemotactic and mitogenic for bone and PDL cells and angiogenic, so it drives revascularization. A beta-TCP scaffold is an osteoconductive matrix that keeps soft tissue from collapsing into the defect and stabilizes the clot; the exam-review guide pairs it with rhPDGF-BB. 3 Regeneration vs repair; only histology proves it Core of the slides · 5 questions in the bank The definition on the slides comes from the 1996 World Workshop in Clinical Periodontics: periodontal regeneration is the formation of new bone, new cementum and new periodontal ligament, together forming a new functional attachment apparatus, over a pathologically exposed root surface. All three tissues are required; bone fill alone is not regeneration. The slide sets regeneration against repair, healing that does not restore the original architecture and function. After a flap or root planing, a root usually heals by repair: a long junctional epithelium lies against the root instead of new cementum with inserting ligament fibers. Regeneration is evaluated three ways: histology, clinical measurements and radiographs. Only histology, a section of the tooth with its surrounding tissue, can show new cementum with inserting PDL fibers and new bone, and so prove true regeneration; the deck shows histological evidence of regeneration in intrabony defects. A probe can't tell new attachment from a long junctional epithelium, and a radiograph shows bone fill, not attachment. Digital subtraction radiography lines up two standardized radiographs taken at different times and subtracts one from the other, so only what changed shows. Dr. Geurs and colleagues used it to evaluate a bioresorbable membrane in periodontal bone defects (Chaves, Geurs, Reddy and Jeffcoat, 1996): the subtraction image lights up the bone gained at the distal site between the presurgical film and the one at 6 months. In the same study, histology 6 months after the membrane showed new cementum, a periodontal ligament space and new bone formed into a reference notch cut in the root. 4 Risk factors for a less predictable result Review guide · 3 questions in the bank The periodontal regeneration risk assessment for intrabony defects (Levine, 2023) rates four groups of factors as low, medium or high risk. Patient factors: medical status (healthy, uneventful healing is low; compromised healing is high); smoking (a nonsmoker is low, a light smoker of 10 cigarettes a day or fewer is medium, more than 10 a day is high); plaque control by full-mouth plaque score (15% or less is low, 16 to 24% medium, 25% or more high); compliance with supportive periodontal care (compliant, erratic or poor); and realistic or unrealistic expectations. Tooth factors: the site's periodontal risk score; whether occlusal trauma and mobility are controllable; the endodontic condition (a vital tooth whose defect doesn't reach the apex, or adequate root canal treatment, is low; existing root canal therapy needs careful evaluation and is medium; a defect reaching the apex of a vital tooth, inadequate root canal treatment or a nonvital tooth is high); the root surface (flat is low, concave medium, two fused roots high); intact soft tissue or soft-tissue defects; and the gingival phenotype (thick is low; thin with a band of keratinized tissue 2 mm or wider is medium; thin with a narrow band or none is high). Defect factors: a 3-wall, narrow, deep defect is low, a 2-wall defect medium, and a 1-wall, wide, shallow defect high; no furcation involvement is low, Class I or II medium, Class III high; the defect must be cleansable through surgical access (anterior is low, posterior medium); and a contained defect, with 1 or 2 sides of the root involved, is low, while a non-contained defect, with 3 or more sides involved, is high. Operator factors: experience, environmental stress, and whether a checklist is used. 5 The AAP decision tree Core of the slides · 5 questions in the bank The decision tree from the AAP Regeneration Workshop (Reynolds, 2015) starts with the patient: address first uncontrolled systemic conditions, tobacco use and other behavioral issues, and inadequate oral hygiene. These are the same factors that ruled furcation regeneration out in Session 5. After initial therapy and any occlusal trauma or mobility management, assess the site: probing depth and CAL, bleeding on probing, mobility and fremitus, the osseous architecture clinically and on radiographs, and any restorative, endodontic or orthodontic work. An intrabony defect under 3 mm isn't a regeneration case: with probing depths of 5 mm or less and no bleeding, consider non-surgical management; with probing depths over 5 mm, consider osseous surgery. For a defect of 3 mm or more, predictability runs 3-wall, then circumferential or 2-wall, then 1-wall, and narrow beats wide. If the prognosis with treatment is unfavorable, or poor to hopeless, the answer is extraction and tooth replacement. Otherwise regeneration follows the defect: a 3-wall or circumferential defect under 2 mm wide takes a bone graft, a GTR membrane or a biologic; one 3 mm or wider, or a 2-wall defect, takes a reinforced GTR membrane, a bone graft plus a GTR membrane, or a bone graft plus a biologic; a 1-wall defect takes combination therapy or a cellular bone allograft. Esthetic risk is weighed alongside. With low risk (a low smile line, a thick biotype, a full papilla, under 5 mm from the contact to the interproximal bone crest), proceed. With high risk (a high smile line, a thin biotype, papilla loss or more than 6 mm from the contact to the crest), proceed only if the patient accepts the esthetic risk, avoid a GTR membrane, and consider soft-tissue augmentation. 6 Graft types and the GTR membrane Core of the slides · 4 questions in the bank Bone grafts. The deck's graft case used DFDBA, demineralized freeze-dried bone allograft: bone from a human tissue-bank donor. The defect was filled, and after healing the site probed 3 mm. Grafts are named by where they come from: an autograft from the patient, an allograft from another human, a xenograft from another species, such as bovine bone, and an alloplast, a synthetic material such as beta-tricalcium phosphate. Guided tissue regeneration. A barrier membrane goes over the defect, under the flap. It keeps the fast-growing gingival epithelium and connective tissue off the root, so cells from the PDL and bone can repopulate it. In combination therapy a bone graft goes under the membrane and holds the space, so the membrane can't collapse into the defect. The deck follows GTR and graft cases with radiographs at 1 year, 20 years and 25 years: the regenerated bone was still there decades later.
